title: LinkedIn Lead Magnets for B2B Founders: Examples and Follow-Up
summary: Build LinkedIn lead magnets that help B2B buyers make decisions. Explore five formats, a worked example, distribution options, and practical follow-up.
body_markdown:
A LinkedIn lead magnet is a useful resource you share through LinkedIn to attract potential customers and give them a reason to continue the conversation. It might be a checklist, worksheet, template, or small tool. You can make it freely accessible or ask people to submit a form to receive it.


For a B2B founder, the resource should help a specific buyer make progress on a problem connected to your business. A thousand people downloading a general productivity guide tells you little about demand for your infrastructure product. A smaller group using a migration checklist may give you something more relevant to learn from.


The practical question is what your buyer needs to figure out before they are ready to talk to you.


This guide covers organic LinkedIn distribution. It explains how to choose a resource, promote it, and follow up. Paid campaigns and LinkedIn Lead Gen Forms require a separate plan.


## Start with a buying decision you understand


Choose a reader in a recognizable situation. "Engineering leaders" is a broad audience. "An engineering leader deciding whether to replace a homegrown reporting pipeline" gives you a problem to work with.


Look through questions that recur in sales conversations, onboarding, or product evaluations. Which ones can you answer with something a buyer could actually use?


Examples include:


- What should we compare before building this ourselves?
- What needs to be ready before implementation starts?
- How do we know whether our current process needs replacing?
- What should we ask a vendor that the demo will not show us?


Choose the question where your team has useful experience and enough evidence to give a responsible answer. Keep private customer details out of the resource.


The resource should also connect naturally to what you sell. If you provide infrastructure software, a checklist about evaluating infrastructure can demonstrate your judgment. A collection of generic AI prompts may attract attention from people with no relevant problem.


Rethoric's guide to[turning sales objections into LinkedIn content](https://www.rethoric.com/blog-posts/sales-objections-linkedin-content) can help identify questions worth developing.


## Five LinkedIn lead magnet examples for B2B founders


These are illustrative concepts. They are not claims about Rethoric clients or campaign results.


### 1. A buyer evaluation checklist


Example: "Questions to Ask Before Replacing Your Data Pipeline."


Help a technical buyer examine dependencies, migration work, access requirements, and ongoing ownership. Explain why each question matters instead of presenting a long list of boxes to tick.


This format fits a buyer who knows the problem but needs a better way to evaluate possible solutions. Include questions that might reveal your own product is a poor fit. The checklist will be more credible if it makes room for an honest comparison.


### 2. A build versus buy worksheet


Example: "Compare an Internal Build With a Vendor Using the Same Assumptions."


Give the reader a structure for comparing their current workaround, an internal build, and a purchased solution. Include maintenance, support, dependencies, and switching costs alongside the initial expense.


Let readers enter their own assumptions. If you include a worked example, label the numbers as hypothetical. Do not fill the sheet with estimates designed to make buying your product the inevitable answer.


### 3. An implementation planning template


Example: "Plan Your First Workflow Rollout."


Create a short template with space for the internal owner, required access, data preparation, pilot scope, acceptance criteria, and unresolved dependencies.


This is useful when the buyer understands the product but struggles to picture the work involved. A completed example can help, provided it is fictional or approved for public use.


### 4. A diagnostic worksheet


Example: "Find the Manual Handoffs in Your Reporting Process."


Ask the reader to map where information changes hands, where work waits, and who handles exceptions. End with a way to identify what needs further investigation.


Avoid inventing a precise readiness score or declaring that every low score requires your product. A diagnostic should make uncertainty visible, not disguise a sales recommendation as an objective assessment.


### 5. An annotated teardown


Example: "How to Review a Product Demo for the Workflow You Actually Need."


Walk through a public or fictional example and explain what you would examine, what is missing, and which questions remain unanswered.


This format is useful when the founder's expertise is easier to demonstrate than summarize. Use material you have permission to reproduce, and separate observable facts from your interpretation.


## Build a small resource someone can finish


A useful first version solves one problem well enough for someone to act. It does not need to become an ebook.


Take the build-versus-buy worksheet. Start with the decision at the top: "How should we support this workflow over the next year?" Then give the reader three options to compare: keep the current process, build internally, or buy.


For each option, ask:


1. Who owns delivery and ongoing maintenance?
2. Which requirements must work on day one?
3. What will implementation require from the team?
4. Who handles exceptions, support, and changing requirements?
5. Which costs are known, estimated, or still missing?
6. What would make this option unsuitable?


Include an "unknown" field. That is often the most useful part of the exercise because it shows what the buyer needs to investigate before comparing totals.


Add brief instructions and one clearly labeled example row. Check that someone unfamiliar with your product can complete the worksheet without booking a call.


Before promoting it, ask a colleague who understands the buyer to try it. Watch where they need clarification. Fix those gaps before adding more pages or spending time on elaborate design.


## Choose how people will get it


The delivery method changes what the reader has to do and what you can observe.


### Give people a direct link


A public resource page is a straightforward option when you want people to use and share the material easily. You can introduce it in a post and make it available from the founder's Featured section.


You will learn less about individual visitors than you would from a form. Decide whether that tradeoff is acceptable before treating missing email addresses as a failure.


### Use a short form


A form can make sense when you need an email address to deliver the resource or when identifying relevant interest is part of your plan.


Explain what the person receives and what happens afterward. Ask only for information you need. If you also offer a newsletter or sales contact, make that choice clear rather than silently treating a download as permission for everything else.


Test the complete path yourself: mobile page, form, confirmation, email, and access to the resource. A polished post cannot fix a broken download.


### Deliver it in a relevant conversation


If someone asks for the resource, send it with enough context to help them use it. Avoid making them complete an unexpected sequence of follows, comments, and connection requests first.


LinkedIn says it is reducing low-substance posts and engagement bait, including prompts such as "comment to agree." That does not establish a blanket ban on every resource request. It does make a useful, substantive post a better foundation than an empty teaser built around a comment keyword. See[LinkedIn's feed update](https://news.linkedin.com/2026/ImprovingTheFeed) .


## Write a post that is useful before the download


Show the buyer why the resource exists. Name the decision, explain one easy-to-miss detail, and give a preview of the work the resource helps them do.


Here is illustrative copy for the build-versus-buy worksheet. Use it only if the resource has actually been created and the author agrees with the reasoning:


A build-versus-buy comparison can look cheap because the maintenance work has no owner yet.


Before comparing prices, put a name next to support, changing requirements, and the next integration. Then use the same requirements to assess keeping the current process, building internally, or buying.


The worksheet below gives you a place to compare those responsibilities and mark the assumptions you still need to check.


It is for engineering leaders evaluating an internal workflow. There are no preset cost savings or preferred answer.


Open the worksheet using the link below.


The post explains the point even if the reader never clicks. The resource extends the explanation with something they can use.


After launch, return to the topic when you have something useful to add: an example of a missing assumption, a buyer question, or a correction to the worksheet. Each post can lead to the same resource without repeating the same announcement.


Keep the resource connected to your broader[LinkedIn inbound marketing approach](https://www.rethoric.com/blog-posts/linkedin-inbound-marketing-for-founders) , rather than making every post a download request.


## Follow up according to what the person actually did


Requesting a resource tells you they wanted the resource. You need more context before treating them as a sales opportunity.


For someone who explicitly asked you to send the worksheet, a delivery message could be:


Here's the worksheet you asked for. The instructions are on the first tab. If you spot a missing comparison criterion, I'd be interested to hear it.


Deliver the promised material before asking for anything else. If they reply with a specific problem, respond to that problem. For example:


You mentioned that nobody owns maintenance after launch. Is the immediate decision who should own it, or whether to keep the workflow in-house?


A commercial next step can follow when the conversation reveals a relevant need and the person wants help. A download alone is not enough context for a personalized claim that you understand their situation.


Keep follow-up human. LinkedIn's[User Agreement](https://www.linkedin.com/legal/user-agreement) prohibits bots and other unauthorized automated methods for sending messages and performing other account actions. Do not assume a third-party automation is permitted because it is commercially available.


## Measure qualified interest separately from reach


Track what you can observe at each step:


- Distribution: impressions and clicks where those metrics are available.
- Resource access: landing-page visits, completed forms, or tracked downloads, depending on the setup.
- Audience fit: relevant roles and companies among people who identify themselves.
- Conversations: replies that describe a real problem, decision, or timeline.
- Sales progression: accepted meetings and opportunities recorded in your CRM.


Do not infer audience fit for anonymous visitors. Keep a requested download separate from a sales-qualified lead.


Use consistent campaign tags on links where your analytics setup supports them. For example, distinguish a link in the launch post from one in the Featured section. Google's[GA4 URL-builder guidance](https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/10917952?hl=en) explains how UTM parameters identify referring campaigns, with utm_content available to distinguish link variants. These tags help describe recorded traffic; they do not reveal every person who saw the resource or prove that it caused a deal.


Interpret the results as a sequence. Lots of visits with little resource access may point to an unclear landing page or delivery friction. Downloads from unrelated roles suggest the topic or promotion may be too broad. Relevant replies can show where the resource needs another example or a clearer explanation.


Record what prospects tell you directly, too. If someone says they used the worksheet with their team, preserve that context rather than replacing it with a guessed attribution. Rethoric's guide to[measuring LinkedIn content ROI](https://www.rethoric.com/blog-posts/measure-linkedin-content-roi) explains how to separate content activity from evidence of business impact.


Start with one question buyers already ask you. Build the smallest resource that helps them answer it, test the delivery, and use the response to decide what to improve.


If you want help connecting resources like these to consistent founder-led content,[explore Rethoric's LinkedIn consultancy](https://www.rethoric.com/) .


## Frequently asked questions


### What makes a good LinkedIn lead magnet for B2B?


It helps a defined buyer complete a useful task or make a better-informed decision. Checklists, worksheets, and templates can work when they contain relevant expertise and clear instructions. The format alone does not determine quality.


### Should a LinkedIn lead magnet require an email address?


Not always. A direct link makes access and sharing easier. A form gives you more information about people who choose to identify themselves, but adds effort. Choose based on the resource and your follow-up plan, and explain what happens after submission.


### Do I need a large LinkedIn following first?


You can share a resource with a smaller relevant audience or in conversations where it answers a question. A small test can help you improve the asset, but it cannot establish broad demand or guarantee leads.


### Should I ask people to comment to receive it?


Consider whether it helps delivery or simply adds friction. A direct link may be easier. If you invite requests, deliver what you promise and avoid requiring unrelated engagement. LinkedIn's guidance on engagement bait does not mean every comment-based resource offer is prohibited.


### How often should I create a new lead magnet?


Create another when you have a distinct buyer problem worth solving. First check whether the existing resource needs better instructions, a different distribution approach, or an update. There is no universal publishing frequency that guarantees qualified leads.
